CHAPTER 20 — अनन्तज्ञानसागरः (ANANTA-JNANASAGARAH)

Introduction — ज्ञानं सागर इव अनन्तम्

The title of this lesson joins three words: अनन्त (ananta = endless, infinite), ज्ञान (jnana = knowledge) and सागर (sagara = ocean). Knowledge is here pictured as an ocean without a farther shore — however long we sail, new waters always stretch ahead. The lesson's central tension is stated in a famous verse: अनन्तशास्त्रं बहुलाश्च विद्याः अल्पश्च कालः — 'the shastras are endless, the branches of learning many, and time is short.' A senior-secondary student stands exactly at this point: the world of knowledge has opened wide, yet life gives only a few decades to drink from it. What, then, should a seeker do? The Sanskrit tradition answers with three disciplines: choose the essence like the swan (हंसः) that separates milk from water; work steadily like the man who digs a well and surely reaches water; and refine what is heard through श्रवण (listening), मनन (reflection) and निदिध्यासन (deep contemplation). In this lesson (NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit, Course 309) we read an original Sanskrit prose passage on the vastness of knowledge, study five authentic public-domain verses with शब्दार्थ, अन्वय and translation, survey the भारतीय ज्ञानपरम्परा (the Indian knowledge tradition — वेद, वेदाङ्ग, दर्शन and the scientific treatises), and draw grammar (सन्धि, समास, कृदन्त, लकार) from the text itself.

गद्यांशः — An original prose passage (सान्वयं सार्थं च)

ज्ञानं सागर इव अनन्तम् अस्ति। यथा सागरस्य पारं नेत्राभ्यां द्रष्टुं न शक्यते, तथा ज्ञानस्य अपि अन्तः न विद्यते। मानवस्य जीवनं तु अल्पम्, विद्याः च बहुलाः। अतः विवेकी छात्रः हंसः इव सारं गृह्णाति, असारं च त्यजति। यः विनयेन गुरुम् उपगम्य श्रद्धया पृच्छति सेवते च, सः एव विद्याम् अधिगच्छति। विद्यायाः अर्जनं जीवनपर्यन्तं चलति, अतः वयं सर्वदा जिज्ञासवः भवेम। अहङ्कारः ज्ञानस्य महान् शत्रुः; यः 'सर्वं जानामि' इति मन्यते, तस्य विकासः तत्रैव समाप्तः। सागरतीरे बालः इव, विद्वान् अपि ज्ञानसागरस्य तीरे एव तिष्ठति — इति विनम्रता एव सत्यं ज्ञानम्।

शब्दार्थ: सागरः = ocean; इव = like, as; अनन्तम् = endless, infinite; पारम् = the far shore; द्रष्टुम् = to see; न शक्यते = cannot be (done); अन्तः = end; न विद्यते = does not exist; अल्पम् = little, short; बहुलाः = many, abundant; विवेकी = discerning, wise; सारम् = the essence; गृह्णाति = takes, grasps; असारम् = the worthless part; त्यजति = abandons; विनयेन = with humility; उपगम्य = having approached; श्रद्धया = with faith; पृच्छति = asks; सेवते = serves; अधिगच्छति = attains, obtains; अर्जनम् = earning, acquisition; जीवनपर्यन्तम् = lifelong, until the end of life; जिज्ञासुः = one desirous of knowing; अहङ्कारः = pride, ego; शत्रुः = enemy; विनम्रता = humility.

Translation: Knowledge is endless like the ocean. Just as the far shore of the ocean cannot be seen with the eyes, so too knowledge has no end. Human life is short, and the branches of learning are many. Therefore the discerning student, like the swan, takes the essence and leaves the worthless. Only the one who approaches the guru with humility, asks with faith and serves him, attains knowledge. The acquisition of knowledge continues lifelong; therefore let us always remain seekers (जिज्ञासु). Pride is knowledge's great enemy; for one who thinks 'I know everything', growth ends right there. Like a child on the seashore, even the learned person stands only at the shore of the ocean of knowledge — this humility itself is true knowledge.

पञ्च श्लोकाः — Five verses on the ocean of knowledge

1) अनन्तशास्त्रं बहुलाश्च विद्याः अल्पश्च कालो बहुविघ्नता च ।
   यत्सारभूतं तदुपासितव्यं हंसो यथा क्षीरमिवाम्बुमध्यात् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: अनन्तशास्त्रम् = the shastras are endless; बहुलाः = many; विद्याः = branches of learning; अल्पः = little; कालः = time; बहुविघ्नता = there are many obstacles; यत् सारभूतम् = that which is the essence; तत् उपासितव्यम् = that should be pursued/served; हंसः = the swan; यथा = as; क्षीरम् = milk; इव = like; अम्बुमध्यात् = from the midst of water.
   अन्वयः: शास्त्रम् अनन्तं, विद्याः बहुलाः, कालः अल्पः, बहुविघ्नता च (अस्ति)। (अतः) यत् सारभूतं तत् उपासितव्यं, यथा हंसः अम्बुमध्यात् क्षीरम् इव (गृह्णाति)।
   Translation: The shastras are endless, the sciences many, time is short and obstacles are numerous. Therefore one should pursue only what is essential — just as the swan takes the milk alone from the midst of water.
   Theme / Moral: Because knowledge is infinite and life brief, wise selection (सारग्रहणम्) is the first duty of a learner; the swan's क्षीर-नीर-विवेक is the model of discrimination.

2) यथा खनन् खनित्रेण नरो वार्यधिगच्छति ।
   तथा गुरुगतां विद्यां शुश्रूषुरधिगच्छति ॥ (मनुस्मृतिः)
   शब्दार्थ: यथा = just as; खनन् = digging (present participle); खनित्रेण = with a spade; नरः = a man; वारि = water; अधिगच्छति = obtains, reaches; तथा = so; गुरुगताम् = residing in the guru; विद्याम् = knowledge; शुश्रूषुः = one eager to serve/listen.
   अन्वयः: यथा नरः खनित्रेण खनन् वारि अधिगच्छति, तथा शुश्रूषुः गुरुगतां विद्याम् अधिगच्छति।
   Translation: Just as a man digging with a spade reaches water (deep underground), so the student eager to serve and listen obtains the knowledge that resides in the guru.
   Theme / Moral: Knowledge yields itself only to sustained effort and humble service (शुश्रूषा); learning is a digging, not a picking.

3) न चोरहार्यं न च राजहार्यं न भ्रातृभाज्यं न च भारकारि ।
   व्यये कृते वर्धत एव नित्यं विद्याधनं सर्वधनप्रधानम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: न चोरहार्यम् = cannot be stolen by a thief; न राजहार्यम् = cannot be seized by a king; न भ्रातृभाज्यम् = cannot be divided among brothers; न भारकारि = is not a burden (to carry); व्यये कृते = when spent; वर्धते एव = only increases; नित्यम् = always; विद्याधनम् = the wealth of knowledge; सर्वधनप्रधानम् = chief among all wealth.
   अन्वयः: विद्याधनं चोरहार्यं न, राजहार्यं न, भ्रातृभाज्यं न, भारकारि च न; व्यये कृते नित्यं वर्धते एव; (अतः तत्) सर्वधनप्रधानम्।
   Translation: The wealth of knowledge cannot be stolen by a thief nor seized by a king; it cannot be divided among brothers and it is no burden to carry. When spent it only ever grows. Knowledge is therefore the foremost of all forms of wealth.
   Theme / Moral: Unlike material wealth, विद्या is inalienable and grows by sharing — teaching others deepens one's own knowledge.

4) विद्या ददाति विनयं विनयाद्याति पात्रताम् ।
   पात्रत्वात् धनमाप्नोति धनात् धर्मं ततः सुखम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: विद्या = knowledge; ददाति = gives; विनयम् = humility; विनयात् = from humility; याति = attains; पात्रताम् = worthiness; पात्रत्वात् = from worthiness; धनम् = wealth; आप्नोति = obtains; धर्मम् = righteousness; ततः = from that; सुखम् = happiness.
   अन्वयः: विद्या विनयं ददाति; विनयात् पात्रतां याति; पात्रत्वात् धनम् आप्नोति; धनात् धर्मं, ततः सुखम् (आप्नोति)।
   Translation: Knowledge gives humility; from humility comes worthiness; from worthiness wealth; from wealth righteous conduct, and from that, happiness.
   Theme / Moral: The very first fruit of true learning is विनय (humility) — the fitting response of a finite mind before an infinite ocean. Learning that breeds arrogance has failed at its first step.

5) काव्यशास्त्रविनोदेन कालो गच्छति धीमताम् ।
   व्यसनेन च मूर्खाणां निद्रया कलहेन वा ॥
   शब्दार्थ: काव्यशास्त्रविनोदेन = in the enjoyment of poetry and shastra; कालः = time; गच्छति = passes; धीमताम् = of the wise; व्यसनेन = in vice/addiction; मूर्खाणाम् = of fools; निद्रया = in sleep; कलहेन = in quarrel; वा = or.
   अन्वयः: धीमतां कालः काव्यशास्त्रविनोदेन गच्छति; मूर्खाणां (कालः) व्यसनेन निद्रया कलहेन वा (गच्छति)।
   Translation: The time of the wise passes in the delight of poetry and learned works; the time of fools passes in vice, sleep or quarrel.
   Theme / Moral: Since time (काल) is the scarcest resource of the learner, how we habitually spend it decides whether we become धीमान् or मूर्ख.

भारतीय ज्ञानपरम्परा — The Indian knowledge tradition

The image of the ocean is not an exaggeration: the Sanskrit tradition itself maps an enormous continent of knowledge. At its head stand the four वेदाः — ऋग्वेदः (hymns), यजुर्वेदः (sacrificial formulae), सामवेदः (melodies) and अथर्ववेदः (spells, healing and daily life). To study them correctly the tradition developed six auxiliary sciences, the षड् वेदाङ्गानि: शिक्षा (phonetics — correct pronunciation), कल्पः (ritual procedure), व्याकरणम् (grammar), निरुक्तम् (etymology), छन्दः (prosody/metre) and ज्योतिषम् (astronomy and time-reckoning). On the reflective side arose the six systems of philosophy, the षड्दर्शनानि: सांख्यम्, योगः, न्यायः, वैशेषिकम्, मीमांसा and वेदान्तः — six disciplined attempts to answer what reality, knowledge and liberation are. Alongside these, India produced rigorous scientific treatises: चरकसंहिता and सुश्रुतसंहिता in आयुर्वेद (medicine and surgery), आर्यभटीयम् of आर्यभटः and लीलावती of भास्कराचार्यः in गणितम् and खगोलविज्ञानम् (mathematics and astronomy), कौटिल्यस्य अर्थशास्त्रम् in statecraft and economics, and भरतमुनेः नाट्यशास्त्रम् in dramaturgy, music and aesthetics. The Panchatantra opens by calling grammar alone अनन्तपारं किल शब्दशास्त्रम् — 'the science of words is indeed shoreless.' If a single shastra is shoreless, what of the whole ocean? The lesson for the modern student is double: pride ('I have finished learning') is absurd, and despair ('I can never learn it all') is unnecessary — the tradition never asked anyone to drink the ocean, only to fill one's own vessel with its essence.

साधकस्य मार्गः — The learner's path: श्रवण, मनन, निदिध्यासन

How should a seeker actually learn, standing before this ocean? The Upanishadic tradition (बृहदारण्यक-उपनिषद्) prescribes a threefold discipline: श्रोतव्यः मन्तव्यः निदिध्यासितव्यः — (the truth) 'should be heard, should be reflected upon, should be deeply contemplated.' (1) श्रवणम् — attentive listening/study at the feet of a teacher: receiving knowledge accurately, with विनय and श्रद्धा, as the शुश्रूषु of Manu's verse does. (2) मननम् — independent reflection: turning what was heard over in one's own mind, raising doubts, testing it with reason (युक्ति) until it is one's own and not merely borrowed. (3) निदिध्यासनम् — sustained, repeated contemplation until the knowledge settles from the mind into character and conduct. Modern learning science says the same in other words: attend, question, and repeatedly retrieve. To these the tradition adds the ethic of lifelong learning: because the ocean is infinite, स्वाध्याय (self-study) is a daily duty that never ends — the Taittiriya Upanishad's parting instruction to students is स्वाध्यायान्मा प्रमदः, 'do not neglect self-study.' The seeker's attitude is therefore a paradox held in balance: infinite ambition (keep learning till the last day) and radical humility (know that what remains unlearnt is always greater).

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the text

(A) सन्धिः. Examples from the verses: बहुलाश्च = बहुलाः + च (विसर्गसन्धिः — visarga before च becomes श्); वार्यधिगच्छति = वारि + अधिगच्छति (यण्-सन्धिः — इ + अ → य्); क्षीरमिवाम्बुमध्यात् = क्षीरम् + इव + अम्बुमध्यात् (दीर्घसन्धिः — अ + अ = आ in इव + अम्बु); तदुपासितव्यम् = तत् + उपासितव्यम् (व्यञ्जनसन्धिः — त् before a vowel becomes द्); विनयाद्याति = विनयात् + याति (त् → द् before य्); नास्ति = न + अस्ति (दीर्घसन्धिः). Splitting such joins (सन्धिविच्छेदः) is the first skill of reading.

(B) समासः. ज्ञानसागरः = ज्ञानम् एव सागरः (कर्मधारयः, a metaphor-compound: knowledge itself pictured as the ocean); विद्याधनम् = विद्या एव धनम् (कर्मधारयः); चोरहार्यम् = चोरेण हार्यम् (तृतीया-तत्पुरुषः); राजहार्यम् = राज्ञा हार्यम् (तृतीया-तत्पुरुषः); गुरुगताम् = गुरुं गताम् (द्वितीया-तत्पुरुषः); काव्यशास्त्रविनोदः = काव्यं च शास्त्रं च (द्वन्द्वः) तयोः विनोदः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः) — a compound inside a compound; सर्वधनप्रधानम् = सर्वधनेषु प्रधानम् (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुषः).

(C) कृदन्ताः (participles and verbal derivatives). खनन् = 'digging', शतृ-प्रत्ययः (present active participle of खन्); उपासितव्यम्, श्रोतव्यः, मन्तव्यः, निदिध्यासितव्यः = 'should be pursued / heard / reflected on / contemplated', तव्यत्-प्रत्ययः expressing duty (विधि); कृते in व्यये कृते = क्त-प्रत्ययः, and the phrase व्यये कृते is a सति-सप्तमी (locative absolute): 'when spending has been done'; शुश्रूषुः = a desiderative (सन्नन्त) noun from सेव्/श्रु — 'one who desires to serve/hear'; द्रष्टुम् = तुमुन्-प्रत्ययः, infinitive 'to see'.

(D) लकाराः. गच्छति, ददाति, आप्नोति, अधिगच्छति = लट्-लकारः (present tense, प्रथमपुरुषः एकवचनम्); वर्धते, सेवते = लट्-लकारः आत्मनेपदम्; भवेम = विधिलिङ्-लकारः उत्तमपुरुषः बहुवचनम् ('may we become'); tense of duty is carried not by a लकार but by the तव्यत् forms above.

सारांशः (SUMMARY)

In this chapter you learned that knowledge is an ocean without a far shore — अनन्तशास्त्रं बहुलाश्च विद्याः अल्पश्च कालः — and that the learner's response must be neither pride nor despair but discriminating, humble, lifelong effort. You read five public-domain verses: on choosing the essence like the swan, on digging for knowledge like a well-digger (मनुस्मृति), on विद्याधन as the supreme, unstealable wealth that grows when spent, on विद्या ददाति विनयम् (knowledge's first gift is humility), and on how the wise and the foolish spend time. You surveyed the भारतीय ज्ञानपरम्परा — four वेद, six वेदाङ्ग, six दर्शन and the great scientific treatises (चरकसंहिता, सुश्रुतसंहिता, आर्यभटीयम्, लीलावती, अर्थशास्त्रम्, नाट्यशास्त्रम्). You learned the seeker's threefold discipline श्रवण-मनन-निदिध्यासन and the duty of daily स्वाध्याय. Finally you drew grammar from the text: विसर्ग/यण्/दीर्घ/व्यञ्जन सन्धि, तत्पुरुष-कर्मधारय-द्वन्द्व समास, the कृदन्त forms (शतृ, तव्यत्, क्त, तुमुन्, सन्नन्त) and the लट् and विधिलिङ् लकाराः. The ocean remains infinite; your vessel, filled daily with its essence, need never be empty.

topics.name: अनन्तज्ञानसागरः — The Infinite Ocean of Knowledge
topics.description: The central theme of the chapter: knowledge is an ocean without a far shore while human life is short (अनन्तशास्त्रं बहुलाश्च विद्याः अल्पश्च कालः); why this calls for wise selection of the essence (सारग्रहण), humility, and lifelong effort rather than pride or despair.

topics.name: Selected Verses on Knowledge and their Meanings
topics.description: Five authentic public-domain verses — अनन्तशास्त्रं बहुलाश्च विद्याः, यथा खनन् खनित्रेण (मनुस्मृति), न चोरहार्यं न च राजहार्यम्, विद्या ददाति विनयम्, and काव्यशास्त्रविनोदेन — with their imagery (swan, spade, unstealable wealth) and central ideas.

topics.name: शब्दार्थ, अन्वय and Translation
topics.description: Word-by-word शब्दार्थ of the prose and verses, arranging verse words into natural prose order (अन्वय), and translating Sanskrit passages into clear English — the core comprehension skills of the chapter.

topics.name: भारतीय ज्ञानपरम्परा — The Indian Knowledge Tradition
topics.description: A survey of the tradition's map of knowledge: the four वेद, the six वेदाङ्ग (शिक्षा, कल्प, व्याकरण, निरुक्त, छन्द, ज्योतिष), the six दर्शन, and scientific treatises such as चरकसंहिता, सुश्रुतसंहिता, आर्यभटीयम्, लीलावती, अर्थशास्त्रम् and नाट्यशास्त्रम्.

topics.name: साधकस्य मार्गः — श्रवण, मनन, निदिध्यासन and Lifelong Learning
topics.description: How a seeker should learn: the Upanishadic threefold discipline of श्रवण (attentive listening), मनन (independent reflection) and निदिध्यासन (deep contemplation), the ethic of daily स्वाध्याय, humble service of the guru (शुश्रूषा), and learning as a lifelong duty.
